newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Red Cross urges ethics as relief business booms.
newsitem.headline: Red Cross urges ethics as relief business booms.

text.p: The Red Cross called on Wednesday for a new code of conduct for aid agencies to avoid abuses in their scramble for a slice of the unregulated multi-billion-dollar relief industry.
The need for professionalism was greater than ever, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) said in a major report.
Agencies were taking the place of governments in caring for victims, amidst donor fatigue and big cuts in welfare budgets.

"It's the independent agencies who actually deliver most of the humanitarian assistance in international relief, not the governments, not the United Nations," said Peter Walker, disaster policy coordinator at the Geneva-based body.
"That's an unprecedented power for a very large number of organisations, and with that power has to come responsibility."
The number of aid agencies is booming as militarised internal conflicts proliferate, from Rwanda to Somalia and from former Yugoslavia to Zaire, now renamed the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Agencies have poured more money into Africa than the World Bank. Globally, their number has soared from 28,900 in 1994 to at least 50,000 now, the IFRC said.
Aid bodies can find themselves competing "at the sharp end" in disasters with an array of groups, including military forces, corporations, human rights and conflict-resolution bodies.
"The battle for funds, media profile and market share appears unstoppable," the report said.

"The fear is for values when politics, buying influence, drawing lines on maps can.... make funding conditional. Contracts are replacing old no-strings grants for agencies. If agencies bid for contracts...where is independence?"

The need for universal standards of professional behaviour was nowhere more visible lately than in Rwanda, where the Hutu-led genocide of Tutsis in 1994 gave rise to a Hutu refugee crisis that aid workers dubbed a "disaster merry-go-round".
On the heels of a handful of major agencies providing the bulk of aid came swarms of other groups, many accused of using Rwanda's misery for their own ends in the chaos.
One American organisation that has since disappeared was accused by U.N. officials at the time of trying to scoop up orphaned children for adoption abroad, against Rwandan law.
Others were accused of using medical care as a cover to push religion, or stuffing minors into orphanages to raise funds.

The IFRC said an international study of the Rwanda crisis in 1996 found that almost a third of the 170 aid agencies registered in the region had disappeared. Some $125 million of aid funds, from a total of $1.4 billion, remained unaccounted for.
More recently in eastern Zaire, one agency was trying to raise funds for Rwandan Hutu refugees using a picture of a Tutsi child survivor of the 1994 genocide, with a machete wound to his head.
Aid agencies have played an important role in shaping media coverage of conflicts. Journalists often turn to them for help, which may include transport and accommodation.

But the IFRC said they risked losing credibility if they failed to speak with one voice, as in eastern Zaire late last year when some were accused of deliberately exaggerating the extent of the crisis in their race to raise funds.

Walker said leading aid agencies would start work next month on a new code of conduct to create standards which donors and victims can use to judge humanitarian performance. A detailed manual could be published within a year, he said.
This may discourage new entrants to the aid market, where seven or eight leading agencies account for 75 percent of the emergency response capacity worldwide, he added.
